analysis.one_liner: Requires OSHA to issue an emergency COVID-19 workplace safety standard for high-risk workers.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on the bill; it sat in two committees until the Congress ended, despite 120 cosponsors including 4 Republicans.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ordered the Labor Department to issue, within 7 days, a legally enforceable emergency standard protecting health care workers, paramedics, and other high-risk employees from catching COVID-19 at work. It also required a permanent standard for infectious-disease exposure within two years, mandated employers track and report workplace infections and deaths, and banned employers from punishing workers who raise safety concerns. The House referred it to two committees and never acted again.
analysis.who_benefits: Health care workers, nurses, nursing home staff, paramedics, emergency responders, and other employees at elevated risk of workplace COVID-19 exposure would gain enforceable protections: required exposure-control plans, tracking of workplace infections and deaths, and protection from retaliation for reporting hazards. Workers in states without their own state OSHA plans would get federal coverage the law currently does not provide.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Health care, EMS, and other high-risk workers

how_it_helps.text: Requires OSHA to issue an emergency temporary standard within 7 days of enactment covering health care, paramedic/EMS, and other high-risk workers, remaining in force until a final standard takes effect.
Requires a permanent OSHA standard within 24 months protecting those workers from exposure to infectious pathogens, including novel ones.
Requires employers to adopt infectious-disease exposure control plans with worker input, and to record and report all work-related COVID-19 infections and deaths.
Prohibits employers from retaliating against workers who report violations or hazards to the employer, a government agency, or the media, or who use higher-level protective equipment voluntarily.
Directs the CDC and NIOSH to collect, investigate, and publicly report data on COVID-19 cases among workers in these occupations.

analysis.who_pays: Employers in the health care, EMS, and other high-exposure sectors — hospitals, nursing homes, ambulance services — would bear the cost of buying protective equipment, writing exposure-control plans, and reporting infections. The bill lets OSHA ease enforcement where compliance is not feasible, such as genuine PPE shortages, if the employer shows good-faith effort.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hospitals, nursing homes, and EMS employers

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs would fall on health care employers already financially strained during the pandemic, including PPE procurement at a time of severe supply shortages — a burden the bill itself acknowledges by allowing OSHA enforcement discretion for infeasible requirements.

The bill waives several regulatory review requirements (the Regulatory Flexibility Act, Paperwork Reduction Act, Unfunded Mandates Reform Act, and Executive Order 12866) for the emergency standard, limiting the usual cost and small-business impact analysis before it takes effect.
The emergency standard covers only workers in high-risk occupations and sectors, leaving lower-risk workers without mandated protections.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For nurses, paramedics, and nursing home staff — the occupations with some of the highest infection rates early in the pandemic — enforceable safety requirements and anti-retaliation protections addressed a real, documented risk. The main cost is compliance expense for employers, partly mitigated by the bill's own enforcement-discretion clause for PPE shortages. The design is focused rather than sweeping, but its waiver of normal regulatory review and its 7-day deadline would have forced rapid rulemaking with little deliberation.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Education and Labor and Energy and Commerce committees the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or markup, and died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Scott introduced the bill on April 21, 2020, during the first months of the pandemic, with a large group of original cosponsors.
It was referred the same day to the Committee on Education and Labor and, for relevant provisions, to the Committee on Energy and Commerce.
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote appears in the action history, and the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
The bill drew 120 cosponsors — 116 of 231 House Democrats and 4 of 197 House Republicans — but that support never translated into a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of high-exposure workers — hospitals, nursing homes, ambulance and EMS operators — were better off, since they never faced a federally enforceable COVID-19 workplace standard or mandated infection reporting. Workers in high-risk occupations got no federal standard from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals, nursing homes, and EMS employers

for.name: Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a large bloc of original cosponsors.

against.name: House Education and Labor and Energy and Commerce Committees
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral — no hearing or markup appears in its action history.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory OSHA emergency COVID-19 standards during the 2020 pandemic response, and only 4 of 197 House Republicans cosponsored.

against.name: Trump administration Labor Department
against.what_they_did: Declined to issue an OSHA emergency temporary standard for COVID-19, issuing non-binding guidance instead, and defended that choice against union lawsuits.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship split sharply by party: 116 of 231 House Democrats signed on versus 4 of 197 House Republicans, and the bill never reached the floor of the Democratic-controlled House or the Republican-controlled Senate.

industries.note: The bill would have required these employers to buy protective equipment, write exposure-control plans, and report every work-related infection and death. Their interest in avoiding those mandates during a PPE shortage ran against the protections the bill offered their own workers.

industries.industry: Ambulance, EMS, and emergency response services
industries.note: Explicitly covered by the standard, including services provided by firefighters and other emergency responders. Compliance costs and infection reporting would have fallen on these operators, while their employees would have gained enforceable protections.

industries.industry: Other high-exposure employers (meatpacking, transit, corrections, and similar sectors)
industries.note: The bill covers other workers 'at occupational risk' of exposure, so compliance obligations could extend beyond health care, but the scope of this catch-all category would depend on OSHA's rulemaking.
